Family Health

Shoulder and shoulder-blade pain after breast cancer

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pain around the shoulder or shoulder blade can make dressing, reaching and sleeping difficult. After breast cancer, it may relate to treatment, an ordinary joint or muscle problem, or less commonly cancer that has spread. The location or character of the pain cannot tell you the cause on its own. New, persistent or worsening symptoms deserve an assessment and a plan to improve comfort and movement.

How the shoulder and shoulder blade work together

The shoulder blade, or scapula, is the broad, roughly triangular bone on the upper back. One part forms the socket that meets the upper arm bone. Muscles attached around it help position that socket as you lift, reach or rotate your arm.

The shoulder is therefore more than a single joint. Bones, muscles, tendons, ligaments, nerves and blood vessels work together to create a large range of movement. Changes in posture, muscle strength or the way the shoulder blade moves can affect the whole system.

Surgery and radiotherapy around the breast, chest or armpit can alter nearby tissues and the way you use your arm. Protecting a painful area may also change movement. These effects help explain why discomfort can extend beyond the breast itself.

There is no single percentage that describes shoulder problems after every breast-cancer treatment. Studies use different definitions, procedures and follow-up periods. Your treatment history and current examination are more useful than applying an isolated statistic to your own recovery.

What the pain may feel like

A tight or aching shoulder may be difficult to raise, while a sharp pain may occur during a particular movement. Some people notice reduced lifting strength, stiffness, tenderness or a numb area. A clinician will ask what triggers the pain and whether movement has changed.

Nerve-related symptoms can include burning, tingling, shooting pain or unusual itching. An area may feel numb yet also uncomfortable. These sensations can occur after local nerve disturbance and do not necessarily mean that cancer is active.

Deep, persistent bone pain is another pattern that needs attention, particularly with a history of cancer. However, descriptions such as dull, sharp or burning overlap between conditions. Neither an online checklist nor which shoulder hurts can establish a diagnosis.

Pain may disturb sleep and affect mood; poor sleep and distress can make coping harder in return. These effects are part of the care discussion. They do not make the pain imaginary, and emotional support should accompany rather than replace assessment of its physical cause.

Common shoulder problems still happen after cancer

Tendon irritation, bursitis, arthritis, frozen shoulder and an injury can cause shoulder pain whether or not someone has had breast cancer. A problem in the neck can also contribute to symptoms around the shoulder or arm. Treatment history is important, but it is not the only possible explanation.

An assessment may include your range of movement, strength, sensation, posture and the appearance of the breast, scar and arm. Tell the clinician when the pain began, whether it follows an injury and whether it occurs at rest or at night.

Tests are chosen according to the findings. Some people need imaging or further cancer-team assessment; others need a rehabilitation plan for a joint or soft-tissue problem. Do not assume that all pain is recurrence, or dismiss persistent pain as an inevitable consequence of treatment.

When cancer itself can cause shoulder pain

Shoulder pain alone is not a usual way to identify an early breast cancer. When breast cancer spreads to bone, however, it may cause ongoing pain and weaken the affected bone. A fracture can occasionally occur with little or no injury.

Breast cancer is not the only cancer that can affect bones near the shoulder. Other cancers, including lung, kidney, prostate and thyroid cancers, may also spread to bone. This is a reason to assess a concerning symptom in its clinical context, not to use a list of cancers to diagnose a sore shoulder.

Cancer affecting the liver can sometimes cause pain felt in the right shoulder. This is referred pain: irritation or pressure in one area is experienced elsewhere through shared nerve pathways. Most right-shoulder pain does not establish that the liver is involved.

Tell your cancer team about new or ongoing bone pain, especially if it is worsening or disturbing sleep. Also report symptoms such as yellowing of the eyes or skin, abdominal discomfort, persistent nausea or vomiting, appetite loss or unexplained itching. Prompt review can identify treatable problems and help control symptoms.

Pain after breast or lymph-node surgery

Lumpectomy, mastectomy, lymph-node procedures and reconstruction can all affect comfort and movement around the chest and shoulder. Drains and the healing tissues around them can also be uncomfortable. The type and extent of surgery influence recovery, but even a smaller operation may leave troublesome symptoms.

Small nerves may be stretched, irritated or divided during surgery. This can cause numbness, burning, tingling or sensitivity around the scar, chest, armpit or upper arm. Scar tightness and guarding the area can add to stiffness.

Some discomfort improves as healing progresses; persistent pain can last much longer and deserves treatment. It should not be assumed to occur only after mastectomy or only after extensive lymph-node removal. A clinician can distinguish nerve pain from other causes and suggest appropriate help.

Report increasing redness, warmth, discharge, fever or feeling unwell promptly because these can indicate infection. A new collection of fluid or swelling also needs assessment. Postoperative fluid, lymphoedema and other causes of swelling are not interchangeable diagnoses.

Cording, also called axillary web syndrome

After surgery, a tight band may become visible or palpable under the skin of the armpit, chest or arm. It can be especially noticeable when the arm is raised and may extend towards the elbow or wrist. This is often called cording or axillary web syndrome.

It may develop in the weeks after surgery or become apparent later. Pulling, pain and restricted reach can make everyday tasks difficult. Published estimates vary widely, so a broad percentage range does not predict whether one person will develop it.

Cording often improves, but its duration and recurrence vary. Ask your breast-care team or physiotherapist to assess it and show you suitable exercises. Treatment may include gentle movement and carefully selected hands-on techniques.

Do not try to snap, forcefully stretch or break a cord yourself. A painful restriction should be worked on within a rehabilitation plan, taking account of wound healing, swelling and any other treatment.

Radiotherapy and tissue tightness

Radiotherapy damages cancer cells, but nearby healthy tissues can also be affected. During later repair, some tissues may become firmer and less elastic. This process, called fibrosis, can contribute to tightness, discomfort and reduced shoulder movement.

Effects depend on the treatment area and individual response. Changes may involve the skin, underlying soft tissues or, less commonly, nerves. A stiff shoulder after radiotherapy should still be examined for other possible causes.

The term radiation fibrosis does not mean that every area of tightness is dangerous or that every symptom will progress. Some radiation effects can be serious, but local stiffness alone cannot establish the extent of tissue injury.

Rehabilitation may help maintain or improve function, although no exercise or massage programme guarantees reversal of fibrosis. Report new weakness, progressive restriction or persistent pain so that the team can tailor care and investigate when needed.

Local nerve injury and chemotherapy-related neuropathy

A local nerve affected by surgery or radiotherapy may cause symptoms around the shoulder, chest or arm. Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy is a different pattern of nerve injury and commonly begins in the hands or feet. These problems should not be grouped together as if they have the same location or treatment.

Peripheral neuropathy may cause tingling, numbness, burning, altered temperature sensation or weakness. It can affect writing, fastening clothes, walking and balance. Reduced sensation also makes it easier to miss a burn or other injury.

Report symptoms early, especially while receiving chemotherapy. Your team may need to assess their severity, review treatment and offer pain management or occupational and physical rehabilitation. Do not independently stop cancer treatment or assume that nerve symptoms will always disappear after it ends.

When the shoulder blade appears to stick out

A shoulder blade that protrudes more than usual is sometimes described as winging. It can occur when a muscle that holds the blade against the chest wall is weak or its nerve supply has been injured. Breast or underarm surgery is one possible context.

You may notice a change in the outline of the back, difficulty lifting or rotating the arm, reduced strength or aching and burning with activity. These signs need an examination; a photograph cannot identify the affected nerve or rule out other movement problems.

Recovery varies with the cause and degree of injury. Some people improve with time and targeted rehabilitation, while others need further specialist assessment. It is not reliable to promise that winging will resolve within a few months or to apply one study’s incidence to every operation.

A physiotherapist can assess movement and plan suitable strengthening or support. New or increasing weakness, swelling or a marked change in the shape of the shoulder should be reported rather than worked through with unsupervised exercise.

Physiotherapy and a gradual return to movement

Rehabilitation can combine movement assessment, comfortable stretches, graded strengthening and practical changes to daily activities. Hands-on treatment may be appropriate for some soft-tissue or joint restrictions, but the plan should follow the cause of the symptoms.

Gentle postoperative exercises often begin very early, sometimes the day after surgery. Reconstruction, drains, wound problems and the surgeon’s instructions may change the timing or range allowed. Ask for the programme intended for your operation instead of waiting for a fixed four-to-six-week window.

Progress gradually and tell the team if an exercise causes significant or worsening pain. The aim is useful movement and confidence, not forcing the arm through a restriction. Improving movement can also help you hold the position needed for radiotherapy.

If arm or chest swelling suggests lymphoedema, seek an appropriate assessment. Specialist lymphoedema care may include selected techniques such as manual lymphatic drainage. Ordinary massage is not a substitute for diagnosis or a complete swelling-management plan.

What massage can and cannot offer

Massage or myofascial techniques may help selected people with persistent discomfort and restricted movement after surgery. Their suitability depends on the tissues involved, healing and the person’s wider cancer care. They should not be applied forcefully over an unexplained painful area.

A small 2018 pilot study involved twenty-one women three to eighteen months after breast surgery. It compared targeted myofascial massage with a control massage approach, using two thirty-minute sessions weekly for eight weeks. The findings were promising for pain and mobility, but the study was too small to guarantee the same benefit for everyone.

Discuss massage with your team and use a practitioner who understands cancer rehabilitation. Wounds, fragile skin, suspected infection, unexplained swelling, a clot or weakened bone can change what is appropriate. A research schedule is not a home-treatment prescription.

Medicines and treatment of the underlying cause

Pain relief is chosen according to the cause, severity and effect on daily life. A clinician or pharmacist can advise whether a non-prescription medicine is suitable alongside your other treatments and health conditions. More medication is not automatically the next step when the diagnosis is unclear.

Nerve pain may respond to medicines used specifically for that purpose. Opioids or corticosteroids have roles in selected circumstances, but they are not routine remedies for every painful shoulder. Ask about expected benefits, side effects and when the plan will be reviewed.

If cancer in bone is causing pain, treatment may include cancer-directed therapy, radiotherapy, bone-strengthening medicines or a procedure to stabilise a weakened bone. Rehabilitation must then take fracture risk into account.

Pain that interrupts sleep, movement or everyday care deserves follow-up even when it has been present for a long time. You do not have to demonstrate that you can tolerate it before asking for a better plan.

Symptoms that need urgent help

Seek urgent assessment for sudden severe shoulder pain, an inability to move the arm, a major change in shape, marked swelling, persistent loss of sensation or fever with a painful hot area. A recent injury or operation makes the surrounding circumstances particularly important.

Call emergency services for shoulder or arm pain accompanied by chest pressure, sudden breathlessness, collapse or other symptoms suggesting an acute heart or lung problem. Pain with sweating should not simply be attributed to a breast-cancer treatment.

With a cancer history, new severe or unexplained back pain together with weakness, difficulty walking, numbness or loss of bladder or bowel control is an emergency. Pressure on the spinal cord needs rapid assessment. Do not wait for a routine physiotherapy appointment.

For symptoms without emergency features, contact your cancer team or usual clinician and explain the cancer history, treatment dates and changes in function. Keeping a brief record of pain, triggers and associated symptoms can make that conversation more useful.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Breast-cancer organisations describe pain, altered sensation, cording and movement problems after treatment, while general shoulder guidance also covers common joint and tendon causes. Persistent or new pain needs individual assessment rather than diagnosis from its location.

Rehabilitation and pain treatment are selected according to the cause and surgical restrictions. Research on a particular technique, including a small massage trial, does not establish a universal recovery timetable or guarantee benefit.

How BeMama can help

Use this guide to prepare questions for your cancer or rehabilitation team: what may be causing the pain, which movements are safe, and when the plan should be reviewed.

When to seek help

Seek emergency care for chest symptoms, sudden breathlessness or possible spinal-cord symptoms. Report infection signs, sudden loss of arm function and new or worsening pain promptly.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Shoulder pain after breast cancer has several possible causes; pain alone does not prove recurrence.
  • Surgery, cording, radiotherapy changes and nerve injury can each affect comfort and movement.
  • Rehabilitation timing should follow your operation and clinical advice, with gradual movement rather than force.
  • New, worsening or persistent pain deserves review, and emergency symptoms need immediate help.

Frequently asked questions

Does shoulder-blade pain mean that breast cancer has returned?

No. Muscle, tendon, joint and treatment-related problems can cause similar pain. A cancer history makes it important to report new or persistent symptoms, but the cause requires assessment rather than a conclusion from the location alone.

Can breast surgery affect the shoulder even after a lumpectomy?

Yes. Tissue healing, local nerve disturbance, scar tightness and changes in arm use can occur after different breast operations. Persistent pain is not limited to mastectomy or extensive lymph-node surgery.

What is the tight cord under my arm?

It may be axillary web syndrome, also called cording, which can appear after surgery and restrict lifting. Ask your breast-care team or physiotherapist to examine it. Do not try to break or snap it yourself.

Should I wait a month before exercising my shoulder?

There is no universal waiting period. Gentle exercises often start much earlier, but reconstruction, drains or healing problems can change the instructions. Follow the programme given for your operation and ask before increasing the range or resistance.

Is right-shoulder pain a sign of liver spread?

Liver problems can sometimes cause referred pain in the right shoulder, but this symptom has many other explanations. Persistent pain or accompanying jaundice, abdominal symptoms or appetite changes should be discussed with your team.

Can chemotherapy make my shoulder and hands hurt?

Some chemotherapy medicines cause peripheral neuropathy, usually affecting the hands or feet. Local shoulder or arm symptoms may have another cause, including surgical nerve injury. Report the pattern so your team can distinguish them.

Will a winged shoulder blade return to normal on its own?

Recovery depends on the cause and extent of weakness or nerve injury. Some cases improve, but a fixed recovery date cannot be promised. An examination and an individual rehabilitation plan are appropriate.

Is massage a proven treatment for everyone?

No. A small trial found promising results for a selected massage approach after breast surgery, but it cannot establish benefit for every person or every cause of pain. Check suitability with your team, particularly with swelling, fragile skin or bone involvement.

What if pain affects sleep and mood?

Tell your clinician. Pain, sleep and emotional wellbeing can influence one another, and all deserve support. This does not mean the pain is psychological or that physical assessment should be skipped.

Which symptoms should not wait for an appointment?

Chest pressure, sudden breathlessness, collapse or new neurological symptoms need emergency care. With a cancer history, severe back pain with weakness, difficulty walking or bladder or bowel changes is especially urgent. Sudden loss of arm function, marked swelling or fever also needs prompt assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
